# Idea of progress (knowledge accumulates, the future can be better) (`idea_of_progress`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by reproducibility_open_publication, printing_press, systematic_invention
- Core idea: Knowledge and technique can grow without limit because each generation starts from what the last one recorded, so we can know more than the ancients without being wiser than they were; and with that knowledge, hunger, disease and toil can be reduced. The argument from visible evidence works best: things the revered ancients did not have (in 1490 the compass, gunpowder, printing, spectacles, mechanical clocks, paper) show that they did not know everything. Progress is neither automatic nor permanent; it depends on recording, teaching, open criticism and reward for improvement, and societies have lost skills before.
- Pitfalls:
  - Claiming progress is inevitable or that newer is always better (the 'Whig' view of history)
  - Repeating the 'Dark Ages' myth; medieval Europe added mills, heavy ploughs, clocks, spectacles and universities
  - Confusing growth of knowledge with moral improvement; the 20th century had both antibiotics and industrial genocide
  - Telling a culture that reveres its sages or a golden age that they were ignorant; say instead that we see further by standing on their shoulders
  - Promising results on a timescale the patron will hold the player to
- History: greece: c. 500 BC – Xenophanes: the gods did not reveal everything at first, by seeking men find out better in time; rome: c. 65 AD – Seneca: a time will come when our descendants wonder that we did not know things so plain (Natural Questions VII); china: c. 240 BC – Han Feizi: new times need new measures, do not wait by the stump for another hare; the dominant Confucian view looks back to the sage kings; islamic: c. 900 – al-Razi: later scholars can surpass Galen because they inherit his work; 1377 Ibn Khaldun sees crafts and sciences accumulate within a civilisation but dynasties rise and fall in cycles; europe: c. 1120 – Bernard of Chartres, 'dwarfs on the shoulders of giants'; 1620–1627 Bacon, New Atlantis; 1687 onwards Quarrel of the Ancients and Moderns; 1750 Turgot; 1795 Condorcet
- Read:
  - Condorcet, Esquisse d'un tableau historique des progrès de l'esprit humain (1795)
  - J. B. Bury, The Idea of Progress: An Inquiry into Its Origin and Growth (1920)
  - Joel Mokyr, A Culture of Growth: The Origins of the Modern Economy (2016)
